# How to use this document

Ten steps, roughly sequenced from intuition to implementation. Each step has:

- **Resources** — with links and time estimates.
- **Why this step** — the pedagogical rationale.
- **Homework** — an exercise, usually in R, that exploits your statistical background.
- **Quiz** — self-check questions. Answers are collected in the **Answer Key** at the end (no peeking).

Check off steps by editing the `- [ ]` boxes below, or keep using the interactive tracker.

## Progress checklist

- [ ] Step 1 — Bitcoin whitepaper
- [ ] Step 2 — Visual intuition (3Blue1Brown)
- [ ] Step 3 — Interactive blockchain demo
- [ ] Step 4 — Hash functions, empirically, in R
- [ ] Step 5 — Princeton course (consensus & incentives)
- [ ] Step 6 — Mastering Bitcoin (protocol internals)
- [ ] Step 7 — Build a toy blockchain in R
- [ ] Step 8 — The statistics of mining
- [ ] Step 9 — Ethereum & smart contracts
- [ ] Step 10 — Proof-of-stake & on-chain data analysis in R

---

# Step 1 — Read the Bitcoin whitepaper

**Resource:** [bitcoin.org/bitcoin.pdf](https://bitcoin.org/bitcoin.pdf) — Satoshi Nakamoto (2008), 9 pages, ~1 hr.

**Why:** Everything in crypto descends from this document. It defines the core problem — how mutually distrusting parties agree on a ledger without an intermediary (the *double-spend problem*) — and proposes the full solution: a chain of hash-linked blocks secured by proof-of-work. Section 11 even contains a probability calculation (attacker catch-up as a Poisson/gambler's-ruin problem) you will enjoy.

**Homework:** Reproduce the Section 11 attacker-success calculation in R. Write a function `p_attack(q, z)` giving the probability an attacker with fraction `q` of hash power ever overtakes the honest chain from `z` blocks behind, and plot it for `q ∈ {0.10, 0.25, 0.40}` and `z = 0:12`. Verify Satoshi's claim that with `q = 0.10`, six confirmations gives attack probability < 0.1%.

```{r step1-hw}
p_attack <- function(q, z) {
  p <- 1 - q
  lambda <- z * (q / p)
  k <- 0:z
  1 - sum(dpois(k, lambda) * (1 - (q / p)^(z - k)))
}
```

**Quiz 1**

1. What specific failure of "trusted third party" systems motivates the whitepaper?
2. What does a block's hash commit to, and why does that make history tamper-evident?
3. In Satoshi's model, what stochastic process describes the attacker's progress relative to the honest chain?

---

# Step 2 — Visual intuition: "But how does Bitcoin actually work?"

**Resource:** [3Blue1Brown on YouTube](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bBC-nXj3Ng4) — 26 min.

**Why:** Grant Sanderson rebuilds Bitcoin from first principles: a shared ledger among friends, then digital signatures, then the question "who holds the ledger?", until proof-of-work emerges as the natural answer. Watching it immediately after the whitepaper animates what you just read and cements the *why* behind each design choice.

**Homework:** Without notes, write a one-paragraph explanation (as if to a first-year biostat student) of why signatures alone are insufficient and consensus is still needed. Then check your paragraph against the video's ledger-ordering argument.

**Quiz 2**

1. Digital signatures prevent forgery of transactions. What attack do they *not* prevent?
2. Why does "longest chain wins" translate to "most computational work wins"?
3. What role does the nonce play in a block?

---

# Step 3 — Interactive blockchain demo

**Resource:** [andersbrownworth.com/blockchain](https://andersbrownworth.com/blockchain/) — interactive, ~30 min.

**Why:** A sandbox where you type data into blocks, watch SHA-256 outputs change, break the chain, and re-mine it. Ten minutes of clicking makes hashing, nonces, and immutability tangible — and it prefigures exactly what you will implement in Step 7.

**Homework:** In the demo, tamper with block 2 of a 5-block chain and count how many blocks you must re-mine to make the chain valid again. State the general rule, and explain why the cost of rewriting history grows with the depth of the target block.

**Quiz 3**

1. Changing one character in block *k* invalidates which blocks?
2. In the "distributed" tab, how do the three peers detect that one copy was tampered with?
3. Why is "difficulty" expressed as a required number of leading zeros?

---

# Step 4 — Hash functions, empirically, in R

**Resources:** the `digest` and `openssl` R packages; [SHA-256 overview, ethereum.org intro to cryptography or any standard reference](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SHA-2). ~2 hrs.

**Why:** Cryptographic hashes are the atomic unit of everything that follows, and their defining properties — determinism, preimage resistance, avalanche effect, uniformity — are *statistical* claims you can test empirically. As a statistician, you shouldn't take them on faith; you should simulate them.

**Homework:**

1. **Avalanche effect.** Hash 10,000 random strings, flip one random bit in each, hash again, and compute the Hamming distance between hash pairs (as bits). Plot the distribution — it should be ~Binomial(256, 0.5). Run a goodness-of-fit test.
2. **Uniformity.** Take the first byte of 100,000 SHA-256 hashes and chi-square test against Uniform{0,…,255}.

```{r step4-hw}
library(digest)
h <- function(x) digest(x, algo = "sha256", serialize = FALSE)
# hex string -> bit vector, then Hamming distance; fill in and test
```

**Quiz 4**

1. Define preimage resistance and collision resistance. Which is harder to violate, and why (birthday bound)?
2. If SHA-256 outputs were uniform, what is the expected number of hashes needed to find one with 20 leading zero *bits*?
3. Why must a hash function be deterministic yet behave "as if random"?

---

# Step 5 — Princeton: Bitcoin and Cryptocurrency Technologies

**Resources:** [Coursera course (free)](https://www.coursera.org/learn/cryptocurrency) and the [free companion textbook PDF](https://bitcoinbook.cs.princeton.edu/) — ~11 weeks self-paced; chapters 1–5 are the core.

**Why:** The most rigorous academic treatment available: consensus protocols, mining economics as a game-theory problem, anonymity analysis. It treats the material the way you'd want — with the math shown and incentive-compatibility arguments made precise. This is the backbone of the whole plan; steps 6–8 run alongside it.

**Homework:** After the consensus lectures, write a short memo (½ page) on this claim: "Bitcoin's security is economic, not cryptographic." Identify which attacks are prevented by cryptography (signature forgery) versus by incentives (51% attacks, selfish mining), and where the boundary lies.

**Quiz 5**

1. What is a Sybil attack, and how does proof-of-work neutralize it?
2. Why do miners generally build on the longest chain even though nothing *forces* them to?
3. What is selfish mining, and roughly what hash-power threshold makes it profitable?

---

# Step 6 — Mastering Bitcoin (protocol internals)

**Resource:** [Antonopoulos, *Mastering Bitcoin* — free on GitHub](https://github.com/bitcoinbook/bitcoinbook) — read chs. 1–10, ~15 hrs.

**Why:** Where Princeton gives theory, this gives byte-level engineering: keys and addresses, UTXOs, transaction scripts, the Merkle tree, the mining loop. Use it as a companion reference — dip in whenever the course leaves you wanting implementation detail. The UTXO model in particular is a data structure worth understanding deeply before Step 7.

**Homework:** Draw (or diagram in R with `DiagrammeR`) the life of one coin: coinbase creation → spent into two outputs → one output spent again. Label each UTXO, and show why "balance" is a derived quantity, not a stored one.

**Quiz 6**

1. What is a UTXO, and how does the UTXO model differ from an account/balance model?
2. What does a Merkle root let a lightweight client verify without downloading the full block?
3. Why can a Bitcoin address be derived from a public key but not vice versa?

---

# Step 7 — Build a toy blockchain in R

**Resource:** your own editor; `digest` package. ~50–80 lines, 2–3 hrs.

**Why:** Nothing consolidates the mental model like implementing it. You will represent blocks as lists, chain them by previous-hash, and write a proof-of-work loop searching for a nonce whose hash has *d* leading zeros. Every concept from Steps 1–6 appears in miniature.

**Homework:**

1. Implement `make_block()`, `mine_block(block, difficulty)`, and `validate_chain(chain)`.
2. Tamper with block 3 of a 6-block chain and confirm `validate_chain()` catches it.
3. Record mining time over 200 mined blocks at difficulty 3 and 4 (hex zeros); compare the distributions.

```{r step7-hw}
library(digest)
mine_block <- function(block, difficulty = 3) {
  target <- strrep("0", difficulty)
  repeat {
    block$nonce <- block$nonce + 1
    block$hash  <- digest(paste0(block$prev_hash, block$data, block$nonce),
                          algo = "sha256", serialize = FALSE)
    if (startsWith(block$hash, target)) return(block)
  }
}
```

**Quiz 7**

1. In your implementation, exactly which fields must feed the hash for the chain to be tamper-evident?
2. Why does incrementing difficulty by one hex digit multiply expected mining time by ~16?
3. What is your `validate_chain()` checking that a signature check alone would not?

---

# Step 8 — The statistics of mining

**Resources:** your Step 7 code; [Bitcoin difficulty documentation](https://en.bitcoin.it/wiki/Difficulty). ~3 hrs. This step is pure statistics — your home turf.

**Why:** Mining is a beautiful applied-probability system: each hash attempt is a Bernoulli trial, attempts-to-success is geometric, block arrivals form (approximately) a Poisson process, and the difficulty adjustment is a feedback controller targeting a 10-minute mean. Analyzing it converts qualitative understanding into quantitative fluency — and this is where your background gives you an edge most crypto learners never get.

**Homework:**

1. From your Step 7 timing data, fit geometric/exponential models to attempts and time-to-mine; check fit with QQ plots.
2. Simulate a network of miners as a Poisson process; implement Bitcoin's difficulty-adjustment rule (retarget every 2016 blocks to a 10-min mean) under a scenario where total hash power doubles; plot block-interval drift and correction.
3. Estimate P(two miners solve a block within the same 2-second propagation window) — the natural fork rate — as a function of mean block time.

**Quiz 8**

1. Why is time-between-blocks approximately exponential, and what property of the hash search justifies "memorylessness"?
2. If hash power doubles instantly, what is the expected block interval before and after the next retarget?
3. Why does a shorter target block time mechanically increase orphan/fork rates?

---

# Step 9 — Ethereum and smart contracts

**Resources:** [Ethereum whitepaper](https://ethereum.org/en/whitepaper/) (~1.5 hrs); optionally the [ethereum.org developer docs intro](https://ethereum.org/en/developers/docs/).

**Why:** Ethereum's key move is replacing Bitcoin's restricted script with a Turing-complete virtual machine, turning the blockchain into a general state machine. This is the conceptual bridge from "digital cash" to smart contracts, tokens, and DeFi — and it introduces the account model and the notion of *gas*, an economic solution to the halting problem.

**Homework:** Write a comparison memo (1 page): UTXO vs. account model — how each represents state, handles concurrency/replay protection, and what each makes easy or hard. Conclude with which model you'd choose for a hypothetical "clinical-trial data provenance ledger" and why.

**Quiz 9**

1. Why does a Turing-complete blockchain need gas at all?
2. In Ethereum, what is the difference between an externally owned account and a contract account?
3. What replay-protection role does the account *nonce* play (distinct from a mining nonce)?

---

# Step 10 — Proof-of-stake and on-chain data analysis in R

**Resources:** [ethereum.org proof-of-stake docs](https://ethereum.org/en/developers/docs/consensus-mechanisms/pos/) (~1 hr); a public blockchain data API such as [blockchain.info charts API](https://www.blockchain.com/explorer/charts) or [CoinMetrics community data](https://coinmetrics.io/community-network-data/) (free CSV downloads).

**Why:** Proof-of-stake replaces burned energy with economic stake as the source of Sybil resistance — understanding both models and their trade-offs completes your consensus picture. Then close the loop the way a statistician should: with real data. On-chain data is public, rich, and messy, and analyzing it makes everything concrete.

**Homework:**

1. Download daily Bitcoin block-interval or hash-rate data (CoinMetrics community CSV works well with `readr`) and test whether observed block intervals are consistent with the exponential model from Step 8 — including around known difficulty-adjustment epochs.
2. Compute a Gini coefficient (package `ineq`) of a stake or balance distribution (e.g., a snapshot of validator stakes or address balances) and write three sentences on what wealth concentration implies for PoS security assumptions.

**Quiz 10**

1. In PoS, what plays the role that electricity cost plays in PoW for making attacks expensive?
2. What is "slashing" and which validator behaviors trigger it?
3. Name one security trade-off usually cited *against* PoS relative to PoW, and one against PoW relative to PoS.

---

# Answer Key

<details><summary>Click to expand (do the quizzes first)</summary>

**Quiz 1.** (1) Trusted intermediaries make reversible transactions unavoidable, raising costs and enabling fraud/censorship; the paper seeks non-reversible payments without a trusted party. (2) The block header hash commits to the previous block's hash, the Merkle root of all transactions, timestamp, and nonce; changing any historical bit changes all subsequent hashes. (3) A random walk / gambler's-ruin problem, with the attacker's potential progress modeled via a Poisson distribution.

**Quiz 2.** (1) Double-spending: signing two conflicting transactions spending the same coin. (2) Extending the chain requires finding valid proofs-of-work, so the longest valid chain embodies the majority of expended computation. (3) A free variable miners iterate so the block header's hash lands below the difficulty target.

**Quiz 3.** (1) Block *k* and every block after it. (2) Their root/latest hashes diverge from the honest copies — comparison of hashes, not data, reveals tampering. (3) Leading zeros is equivalent to "hash < target"; more required zeros shrinks the target set, lowering per-attempt success probability.

**Quiz 4.** (1) Preimage resistance: given h, can't find x with H(x)=h (~2^256 work). Collision resistance: can't find any x≠y with H(x)=H(y) (~2^128 by birthday bound) — collisions are "easier," which is why collision resistance is the stronger requirement. (2) 2^20 ≈ 1.05 million. (3) Determinism enables verification by anyone; pseudo-randomness prevents anyone from steering or predicting outputs.

**Quiz 5.** (1) Creating many fake identities to sway a vote; PoW makes influence proportional to computation, which can't be faked by minting identities. (2) Blocks off the longest chain are likely orphaned, forfeiting the reward — following the majority is the incentive-compatible strategy. (3) Withholding found blocks to waste competitors' work; profitable somewhere above ~25–33% of hash power depending on network assumptions.

**Quiz 6.** (1) An unspent transaction output — a discrete "coin" consumed whole when spent; balances are sums over UTXOs rather than stored account fields. (2) That a specific transaction is included in a block, via a log-length Merkle branch. (3) Address = hash of the public key; hash functions are one-way.

**Quiz 7.** (1) At minimum: previous hash, block data (or its Merkle root), and nonce; omit any and tampering there goes undetected. (2) Each additional hex zero divides the target set by 16, so expected attempts (geometric mean 1/p) multiply by 16. (3) Chain linkage integrity — that each block's stored prev-hash equals the recomputed hash of its predecessor — i.e., history, not authorship.

**Quiz 8.** (1) Attempts are i.i.d. Bernoulli with tiny p, so attempt counts are geometric and, at high attempt rates, waiting time is approximately exponential; each hash is independent of all previous ones, giving memorylessness. (2) ~5 minutes until the retarget, then back to ~10. (3) Fixed propagation delay becomes a larger fraction of the block interval, raising the probability of simultaneous solutions.

**Quiz 9.** (1) Without metered computation, an infinite loop in a contract would stall every validating node — gas prices computation and guarantees termination economically. (2) An EOA is controlled by a private key and initiates transactions; a contract account is controlled by code and acts only when called. (3) It orders transactions from an account and makes each signed transaction valid exactly once.

**Quiz 10.** (1) Capital at risk: staked funds that can be destroyed (slashed), plus the cost of acquiring stake. (2) Penalizing provably malicious actions — chiefly double-signing/equivocation (attesting to conflicting blocks); penalties destroy part or all of the stake. (3) Against PoS: "nothing-at-stake"/long-range attack concerns and rich-get-richer stake concentration; against PoW: enormous energy expenditure and hardware/mining-pool centralization.

</details>
